articles.title: In 1984, Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter joined volunteers to renovate 19 homes in New York; 42 years later, their project has helped build 4,496 homes
articles.summary: In September 1984, former US President Jimmy Carter and former First Lady Rosalynn Carter led Habitat for Humanity volunteers to New York, building
articles.body: In September 1984, former US President Jimmy Carter and former First Lady Rosalynn Carter led Habitat for Humanity volunteers to New York, building alongside 19 families in need of safe, affordable housing. That was the inaugural Carter Work Project, now a weeklong event held somewhere in the world each year. According to Habitat for Humanity International, the project has since built 4,496 houses in 14 countries with the help of 112,031 volunteers. Builds have taken place in Africa, Asia, Europe and North America. The 2026 project returned to Atlanta, Georgia, for the first time since 1988, where 24 new homes were built in five days.How did the Carter Work Project expand beyond New YorkAccording to Habitat, some 150 volunteers from the United States and Canada worked alongside future homeowners in Chicago in 1986 to build a four-unit townhouse. In 1987, President and Mrs Carter led 235 volunteers in constructing 14 houses in Charlotte, North Carolina's Optimist Park area. The 1988 project, the timeline says, built 20 homes in Atlanta, Georgia, and renovated another 10 housing units in North Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.Habitat states that more than 1,100 volunteers joined the Carters in 1993 for the first Carter Work Project held entirely outside the United States, with 18 houses built in Winnipeg, Manitoba, and 10 in Waterloo, Ontario. The timeline says the 1996 project marked its first foray into Europe, with the Carters leading construction of 10 homes in Vac, Hungary, alongside homeowners and 500 volunteers from 23 countries. In 1999, Habitat reported that 14,000 volunteers from 32 countries helped build 293 homes in six communities in the Philippines. In 2001, more than 9,000 volunteers from South Korea and other countries worked with homeowners to build 136 housing units in Asan, South Korea.What happened to the Carter Work Project in 2023Habitat states that the Carters left a legacy of dedication to community service and human rights, and that it is honoured that they devoted over 35 years to supporting its mission through their advocacy. The organisation adds that some people assume Jimmy Carter founded Habitat, but that the Carters were its "most famous and tirelessly devoted volunteers".President and Mrs Carter could not attend the 2023 project because of their health. Hundreds of volunteers gathered in Charlotte, North Carolina, to help build 27 homes alongside homeowners. articles.title: Military leadership asks Indian Navy to maintain combat readiness, strengthen maritime surveillance
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The country’s apex defence leadership has urged naval commanders to maintain a high degree of combat readiness and strengthen maritime
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The country’s apex defence leadership has urged naval commanders to maintain a high degree of combat readiness and strengthen maritime surveillance, while underlining its role in safeguarding India’s energy security amid the prevailing situation in West Asia.During the Naval Commanders’ Conference 2026, defence minister Rajnath Singh underscored India’s growing strategic responsibilities in the maritime domain and stressed the need to strengthen maritime surveillance, analytical capability and operational responsiveness.Navy chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan, who gave the inaugural address during the conference, reviewed the prevailing maritime security environment and Navy’s operational posture. He underscored the imperative of maintaining a high degree of combat readiness, agility and responsiveness while accelerating technology absorption and capability development to address contemporary and emerging challenges across the maritime domain.Chief of Defence Staff General N S Raja Subramani acknowledged Indian Navy as a strategic force multiplier and commended its sustained efforts towards technology absorption, Aatmanirbharta and safeguarding India’s energy security. He highlighted the changing character of warfare and emphasised the need for accelerated technology transformation, seamless data sharing, enhanced resilience and sustenance, underpinned by greater jointness and integration across the services.Army chief Gen Dhiraj Seth also interacted with naval commanders and shared perspectives on the contemporary security environment. The interaction focused on further strengthening tri-service synergy, interoperability and integrated responses to emerging security challenges. The discussions reinforced the need for closer coordination and continued exchange of operational lessons among the services towards enhancing joint preparedness, officials said.The engagements with CDS and Army chief provided an opportunity for the naval leadership to exchange perspectives on the evolving character of warfare, capability development and the increasing importance of integrated operations in addressing emerging security challenges.During the remaining sessions of the three-day conference, the naval leadership will undertake detailed deliberations on operations, material, logistics, human resources, training, force development and induction of emerging technologies. Measures to optimise force levels, strengthen combat readiness and accelerate capability development will also be reviewed, it said.

articles.title: Flydubai passenger describes putting attacker in chokehold after cockpit stabbing
articles.summary: Other passengers on the Israel-bound flight described the "terrifying" moment the plane dropped.
articles.body:
Passengers on a flight to Israel have recounted how they subdued a pilot after he stabbed the other pilot and appeared to be trying to disable the plane, while others described the "terrifying" moment they thought they would die.

Appearing in a bloodstained shirt after the ordeal, Yaniv Hayun told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu he realised something was wrong when the aircraft suddenly dropped.

The plane, en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv, plummeted 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes.

"Someone screamed... the light went out," Hayun said in a video posted by the prime minister on social media.

He and others tried to push open the cockpit door, but the pilot who had been stabbed was very close to it, so it was hard to open. Before he collapsed, the injured pilot managed to open the door.

When Hayun and another man entered the cockpit, he said he saw one pilot down and the attacker on the instruments, between the two seats, "trying to destroy the instruments in order to...disable the plane".

"I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and pulled him - first and foremost - outside," Hayun said.

"We pulled him out; it was a matter of seconds. I called out to the Israeli guys with us on the plane - I called them, and two other guys came over to me... we pinned [the attacker] down to keep him secure."

Hayun said he then jumped back into the cockpit and "started pulling the controls".

When asked by Netanyahu whether he knew what he was doing, the passenger answered: "I watch Air Crash Investigation, Mr Prime Minister."

Hayun said the plane then started to level out. By then, two on-duty pilots who had been in the passenger cabin were at the front of the plane, and one told Hayun he was taking control from there.

Netanyahu praised Hayun, calling him a "great hero" and a "lion".

Another passenger, Zvika Meness, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan he helped overpower the attacker, and the passenger and two others "tied him up with his own zip ties and with the multimedia headphones".

"Another pilot who was sitting in the passenger cabin went in to replace the additional pilot, and they essentially landed the plane," he added.

The Flydubai flight eventually landed at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, and the passengers were later taken to Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport on a repatriation aircraft.

They were greeted by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags.

"Thank God I'm alive," passenger Haim Lazarovich told journalists, adding that "the most terrifying moment in this flight was when the pilot loses control".

Oran Choen, an 18-year-old passenger, described the incident as "a very tough moment".

"Maybe it was five minutes, but it feels like hell - I heard my brother behind me scream that we was going to die," he added.

A paramedic from Israel's ambulance service later told the BBC that a number of people were "very emotional and crying as they came off the plane".

The stabbed pilot, Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, was taken to hospital but is in stable condition, according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia.

Netanyahu praised Machchhar as a "true hero" of "extraordinary bravery".

The attacker was arrested and is being questioned by Saudi authorities.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack". No official motive for the incident or further information has been given.

US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu following the incident, saying it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack.

articles.title: Staggering drug haul found at major airport after bizarre attempt to hide evidence
articles.summary: Orlando International Airport police and K-9s intercepted over 200 pounds of marijuana allegedly smuggled on commercial flights from Los Angeles. A security expert shares context.
articles.body: More than 200 pounds of marijuana reportedly made its way onto commercial flights from Los Angeles to Orlando International Airport (MCO) this summer — before police intercepted the drugs in two separate airport busts. The smugglers allegedly attempted to bring hundreds of pounds of bulk marijuana into Central Florida from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), according to police records recently obtained by FOX 35 Orlando. The drugs were intercepted by undercover officers with the Orlando Police Department (OPD) and drug-sniffing K-9s, FOX 35 reported. ONE CANNABIS MISTAKE AT AIRPORT COULD BRING 10 YEARS IN PRISON AND $15,000 FINE Investigators said the suspects used superglue and ripped-off luggage tags to try to evade police, as well as dryer sheets to conceal the smell of marijuana. During one bust, which occurred on May 7, officers found 57.6 pounds of marijuana packed inside 50 vacuum-sealed bags, wrapped in blankets and stuffed with dryer sheets, according to the report. In a second bust on July 1, police found 144.4 pounds of marijuana in suitcases with locks that had been completely glued shut. FOX 35 identified the suspects as individuals in their 20s who are now facing felony drug trafficking charges. TSA OFFICER SEES ALARMING SHAPES ON X-RAY BEFORE STOLEN CIVIL WAR MYSTERY UNRAVELS Keith Jeffries, vice president of K2 Security Screening Group, told Fox News Digital that drug smuggling on commercial flights "can happen in multiple ways." Investigators said the suspects used superglue and ripped-off luggage tags to try to evade police. Those scenarios could include airport or airline employees assisting smugglers or traffickers using drug mules, he said — though he cautioned that it remains unclear how the drugs made it onto the flights in these cases. Jeffries also said law enforcement may have been tipped off about certain individuals or bags by a confidential informant. "It's unknown at this time without talking to law enforcement and getting the specifics," he said. Jeffries, who previously served as TSA's federal security director at LAX and deputy federal security director at MCO, added that drug trafficking "can happen on any domestic route — and it does." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER He said Orlando's status as a major tourist destination, in particular, could make the city attractive to traffickers. "The illegal perpetrators in this [situation] may think and believe that, well, the security must be lax there, which is not the case," Jeffries said. He also noted that TSA officers do not specifically search for illegal drugs, and that suspected narcotics discovered during screening are referred to law enforcement. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "The TSA's administrative search authority is very, very narrow and very specific," Jeffries said. "TSA does not look for illegal narcotics," he added. "They simply say, 'We've got an unknown substance, and we need law enforcement's attention so that law enforcement can validate what it is or is not.'" TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Fox News Digital reached out to the Orlando Police Department for additional information. While the Orlando marijuana was intercepted by local law enforcement, TSA officers have made other unusual discoveries during airport screenings in recent weeks. Earlier in September, TSA officers at Dallas Love Field Airport in Texas discovered a pocketknife concealed inside a tube of toothpaste during routine carry-on screening. articles.title: James Van Der Beek's family raised money after his death; months later, questions emerged over the $4.8 million Texas ranch
articles.summary: James Van Der Beek’s family was still dealing with the financial consequences of his cancer treatment when a fundraising campaign for his widow and six
articles.body: James Van Der Beek’s family was still dealing with the financial consequences of his cancer treatment when a fundraising campaign for his widow and six children began attracting attention. Within days of the actor’s death, the GoFundMe had raised millions of dollars to help with medical bills, living costs and the children’s education. Then details of a Texas property purchase resurfaced. Van Der Beek and his wife, Kimberly, had acquired the 36-acre ranch near Austin for about $4.76 million shortly before his death, according to the San Francisco Chronicle. The timing prompted questions online about why the family needed public donations after such a substantial property transaction. A close friend of the actor later pushed back against the criticism, saying the circumstances behind the purchase were not being understood.James Van Der Beek’s death sparks questions over family finances and fundraisingVan Der Beek died on Feb. 11 at the age of 48, after being diagnosed with colorectal cancer three years earlier. His death was announced by his family, bringing an end to a period in which the actor had spoken publicly about his illness and its effect on his family.In the days following his death, a GoFundMe campaign was established for Kimberly Van Der Beek and their six children: Olivia, Joshua, Annabel, Emilia, Gwendolyn and Jeremiah. The campaign said the prolonged treatment and medical costs had depleted the family’s finances. Money raised was intended to help with day-to-day expenses, outstanding bills and the children's education. According to the GoFundMe campaign it had received nearly $2.9 million.The Texas property had been part of the family’s life for yearsAs reported by San Francisco Chronicle, the ranch at the centre of the discussion was not a newly discovered second home. Van Der Beek and Kimberly had been renting the 36-acre property outside Austin since 2020. The couple completed the purchase on Jan. 9 for $4.76 million. The transaction took place only weeks before Van Der Beek died, making the timing particularly conspicuous once details of the property became public.The family’s connection with the ranch therefore predated the purchase by several years. They had already been living there as tenants, and the eventual transaction changed the arrangement from renting the property to owning it.Mehcad Brooks defends the Van Der Beek familyActor Mehcad Brooks, described as a close friend of the Van Der Beek family, responded publicly after a social media user questioned the GoFundMe in connection with reports about the ranch. Brooks argued that people commenting on the situation did not have a full understanding of what the family had experienced during Van Der Beek’s illness. He also criticised the use of the ranch purchase as a reason to question the family’s financial circumstances.Actor Mehcad Brooks, who called himself one of Van Der Beek's closest friends, responded on Threads that the headlines were "fake AF." He said critics had no idea what the family had been through and urged them to hold back from judging.Van Der Beek had previously spoken about moneyThe actor had also discussed the less visible side of earning money from a successful television career. In a 2012 interview with Today, Van Der Beek said, ‘“There was no residual money.”“I was 20. It was a bad contract. I saw almost nothing from that.”His comments offered some insight into why a long career on television did not necessarily translate into the kind of continuing income audiences might assume from a familiar Hollywood name. Van Der Beek became widely known through Dawson’s Creek and later appeared in films including Varsity Blues. Yet his financial circumstances were more complicated than the public image attached to those roles.His comments from 2012 resurfaced in the context of the family's fundraising because they provided an earlier example of the actor discussing the difference between fame and actual long-term earnings.The actor had begun selling personal career memorabiliaIn the months before his death, Van Der Beek also auctioned items connected to some of the roles that had defined his career. The pieces included a tartan buttoned shirt from the first episode of Dawson’s Creek, a necklace associated with Katie Holmes’ character on the series and shoes he wore in Varsity Blues. These were personal items he had kept for years rather than ordinary possessions being cleared out.In November 2022, in conversation with People Van Der Beek said that he had held on to the memorabilia for years before deciding it was time to part with it. He referred to unexpected changes in his life when explaining the decision.Why the ranch became part of the wider debateThe property purchase and the fundraiser involved two different financial circumstances that became linked after Van Der Beek's death. The family had been renting the Texas ranch for years before purchasing it. The purchase was reported at $4.76 million, while the family's representative said the down payment had been secured with help from friends through a trust. The fundraiser, meanwhile, described the financial strain created by medical treatment and sought money for living expenses, bills and education.Those details do not provide a complete picture of the family's finances, and the supplied reporting does not give a full accounting of the trust, mortgage or the family's assets and liabilities. What is documented is that the ranch had been a long-term rental before it was purchased and that the representative gave a specific explanation for how the family obtained the money needed for the transaction.Van Der Beek leaves behind his wife and six childrenVan Der Beek is survived by Kimberly and their six children. His career had stretched across television and film, with Dawson’s Creek becoming the role most closely associated with his early fame.His final years brought a very different kind of public attention. The actor discussed his cancer diagnosis, continued working and eventually began parting with some of the objects associated with his career. After his death, his family turned to a public fundraiser as it dealt with the costs described in the campaign.The questions about the Texas ranch emerged afterwards, when the property purchase was viewed alongside the GoFundMe. His friend Mehcad Brooks and the family's representative both offered explanations that challenged the assumption that the property's reported value alone showed what money was available to the family. The fundraiser and the ranch consequently became connected in public discussion, even though the available reporting describes different financial arrangements behind each.You use AI every day. articles.title: Three unions to strike at once over job cuts at Glasgow Caledonian University
articles.summary: Lecturers and support staff say the action by the UCU, the EIS and Unison on Thursday will effectively close the university.
articles.body:
Staff at Glasgow Caledonian University are staging strike action, with all three campus unions walking out together for the first time over planned job cuts.

Lecturers and support staff say the action by members of the UCU, the EIS and Unison on Thursday could effectively stop the university from operating.

Management at the university plan to cut about 50 posts and say they have not ruled out compulsory redundancies.

They say the cuts are needed to secure Caley's finances and blame a £33m fall in income over two years, partly due to a drop in the number of international students.

The dispute dates back to March when management announced plans to cut up to 100 posts, blaming a sharp fall in income from international students.

Since then, voluntary redundancies have brought that figure down to about 50 but the sticking point is compulsory redundancies.

The unions want a guarantee that nobody will be forced to leave - but the management has refused to rule it out.

Talks at the conciliation service Acas broke down earlier this month and lecturers went on strike last week.

The unions argue the cuts are a choice rather than a necessity.

They point to what they say are £95m in cash reserves as well as the university's purchase of land in the city centre for about £4.5m, which they say is foolish at this time.

The university says buying and selling land is part of a long-standing strategy.

It has previously highlighted that it is facing a £10m financial deficit in the next financial year and said the cuts are needed to put it back on a "sound financial footing".

A university spokesperson said they were "disappointed" the unions had voted to strike.

They said the measures the unions had suggested as alternatives to compulsory redundancies had largely already been taken and that was why the number of job cuts had been reduced.

"While voluntary measures remain our preferred approach, we cannot rule out compulsory redundancies if the required savings are not achieved," they said.

Unison branch secretary Davena Rankin said compulsory redundancies were not the answer.

"Staff want to support students and help the university succeed, but they need confidence that their jobs are secure," Rankin said.

UCU branch president Karen Lorimer said staff wanted to be welcoming new and returning students but the refusal to rule out using compulsory redundancies left them with no alternative but to strike.

Dr Nick McKerrell, a law lecturer and the branch secretary of the EIS, said there were issues across higher education but Caley was in a strong place financially and there was no need for compulsory redundancies.

This is the biggest day so far of what is an ongoing dispute at the university.

For the first time, all three unions are on strike on the same day.

The unions said it was highly unusual for both the lecturers' unions to be on strike at the same university on the same day.

They said that adding the support staff - who run IT, security, catering and cleaning as well as the library and student welfare - would bring the campus and the university to an effective standstill.

The university has said throughout that it wants to keep disruption for students to a minimum but with so many services affected, that will be very difficult.

Further strike dates are planned stretching to the middle of October.

The lecturers' unions are out again next week, and Unison is expected to stagger action among its members.

Glasgow Caledonian is far from an isolated case.

At the University of Edinburgh, about 3,000 staff have begun five weeks of strikes , running until 30 October, over £140m of cuts.

It's the latest chapter in a bruising year.

Back in March, staff in Dundee, Aberdeen , Strathclyde and Heriot-Watt all walked out in separate disputes.

The underlying problem is money and funding.

Scottish universities get a fixed amount from the government for each Scottish student they teach, and they're not allowed to charge them fees.

For years they've made up the gap with fees from international students.

But we've seen the number of overseas students falling, while the cost of staff, pensions and energy keep rising.

Just a few weeks ago, an expert group working for the Scottish government's review of university funding estimated that the sector is short of around £200m a year .

It also found a repairs backlog of about £1bn.

articles.title: Monsoon deficit at 13%, officially a drought year
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The rainy season in India technically ended on Wednesday, with the summer (southwest) monsoon rainfall during June-Sept period recording a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The rainy season in India technically ended on Wednesday, with the summer (southwest) monsoon rainfall during June-Sept period recording a deficit of nearly 13% - a level of shortfall which is considered a drought. Significantly, this is the fourth lowest seasonal rainfall since 2001 and the 13th lowest since 1901.The situation is likely to be better during winter when northeast monsoon hits south Peninsular India between Oct 15 and Oct 21, with the IMD predicting 'normal' rainfall over Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Karaikal, coastal Andhra Pradesh and Rayalaseema region, Kerala and south interior Karnataka during Oct-Dec period. However, the winter monsoon will bring cheer to limited regions.Though most other parts of India are expected to receive 'below-normal' rainfall during the Oct-Dec period, some areas of northwest India (Punjab, parts of Haryana, Uttarakhand, Himachal and J&K) and southern parts of peninsular India are likely to get "normal to above-normal" rainfall. Incidentally, Punjab and peninsular India had to face huge rainfall deficit during the summer monsoon season, which led to drought in many districts.Winter rain may bring relief to southern IndiaOverall, south Peninsular India receives 30% of its annual rainfall during northeast (winter) monsoon season. TN, Puducherry and Karaikal receive 48% of their annual rainfall during northeast monsoon season. So, normal winter monsoon this year may bring relief to the region, which received the fourth lowest summer monsoon rainfall since 1901.“We cannot forecast exact date of arrival of winter monsoon in south Peninsula at this stage. It generally coincides with final withdrawal of summer monsoon and may hit the region any day during Oct 15-21,” said IMD chief Mrutyunjay Mohapatra. Though India as a whole received nearly 13% less than normal rainfall, east and northeast India faced the highest deficit of 25%, followed by south Peninsula (24%), northwest India (6%) and central India (3%). Mohapatra said there has been a recent trend of east & northeast India consistently reporting decrease in rainfall.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Upping the ante against CEC Gyanesh Kumar and PM Modi, the opposition INDIA bloc Wednesday announced a month-long nationwide agitation starting Oct 2, coinciding with the protest call given by various student bodies, including the Cockroach Janata Party, in Delhi and states. Crucially, the opposition collectively demanded that elections should revert to ballot papers from EVMs, and that pre-SIR electoral rolls be restored for future elections. It also sought an effective appeals mechanism for voters excluded from the rolls. The opposition has sought immediate resignation of the chief election commissioner.After deliberations, Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge announced that the six-day agitation from Oct 2-8 would start with district-level "save democracy" protests. He said opposition MPs will march to the EC office in Delhi on Oct 6.Moving forward, the alliance will hold five major rallies in cities during Oct-Nov, including a mega rally in Delhi on Nov 1. The bloc appealed for expediting SC cases pertaining to SIR and electoral malpractices. To mount pressure, the opposition will seek to meet President Droupadi Murmu in Oct to brief her about their concerns regarding SIR and the Election Commission.The meeting was attended by Sonia Gandhi, Rahul Gandhi, Mamata Banerjee (TMC), Dipankar Bhattacharya (CPI-ML), Omar Abdullah (NC), Supriya Sule (NCP), Tejashwi Yadav (RJD), M A Baby (CPI-M), P Sandosh Kumar (CPI), K C Venugopal (Congress), N K Premachandran (RSP), Thol Thirumavalavan (VCK), Uddhav Thackeray (Sena UBT) and Hemant Soren (JMM).The opposition has for now paused the plan to submit a fresh removal notice against CEC Gyanesh Kumar. Kharge said the opposition agrees that Kumar is working like a puppet, with PM Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah pulling the strings.Rahul Gandhi said he told the leaders of the bloc that they are the "collective defenders" of the Indian Constitution. "It is a personal commitment of all INDIA bloc leaders, we are going to ensure that people who have destroyed Indian democracy are punished," he said.Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee said, "We demand that Gyanesh Kumar must resign immediately. If he is not removed, this movement can go very far..... We have to fight this battle together." "Now it is clear, 'Vanish Kumar' is 'chor' (thief), 'daku' (dacoit)... he has stolen votes, burned, hijacked EVMs... rigged counting.... Gyanesh Kumar must resign immediately," the former Bengal CM said, with Sonia sitting next to her and lauding her remarks.Rahul said there was a feeling in the room that the opposition had been successful in convincing people that elections are "stolen". "There is a new sense of resistance, particularly among young people, that what is going on in India is wrong and needs to be stopped," he added.The 19 parties included Samajwadi Party, CPI-ML, JKNC, JKPDP, JMM, IUML, KC(M), MDMK, VCK, KC(J) and AIFB. RS MP Kapil Sibal also joined Wednesday's meet.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Graduated Driver Licensing: Northern Ireland's young drivers first in UK to get new driving licensing laws
articles.summary: Northern Ireland becomes the first part of the UK to introduce new rules for new drivers in a bid to reduce fatal road crashes involving young people.
articles.body:
Northern Ireland has become the first part of the UK to introduce new rules for new drivers in a bid to reduce fatal road crashes involving young people.

Graduated driver licensing (GDL) , for learner and newly qualified drivers, apply to all new drivers but are particularly aimed at 17 to 23-year-olds.

Among the new rules is that learners must spend at least six months getting driving experience before they can take a practical test.

Newly qualified drivers under 24 will also face restrictions on carrying young passengers at night.

The rule changes were announced in January last year and will see the current speed limit of 45mph for restricted drivers removed.

Drivers who do not follow the restrictions could receive three penalty points or a fine of up to £1,000.

Versions of GDL exist in countries including Australia, the US and Republic of Ireland. Campaigners have called for them to be introduced across the UK.

Police say it will "save lives" but there has been a mixed reaction from young drivers, with some in favour while others, from rural backgrounds, feel frustrated.

However a driving instructor described it as a "terrific" step.

According to official figures, 17 to 23-year-old drivers were responsible for 24% of all collisions in Northern Ireland in 2024, despite only accounting for 8% of license holders.

In the same year there were 251 people killed or seriously injured in collisions involving a young driver, and in 65% of those, the young driver was deemed to be at fault.

In January, the government announced that learner drivers in England and Wales could face a minimum period of up to six months between sitting their theory and practical tests.

However, it stopped short of introducing GDLs, which motoring organisation the AA described as "a missed opportunity".

Earlier this year Scottish ministers called on the government to grant them powers to put their own restrictions on new young drivers.

The UK government said it wanted to keep young people safe but had decided not to introduce "blanket restrictions" on new drivers.

What do young people think of the changes?

For 16-year-old Tommy from Omagh, driving is a "big factor" in his life.

He has been learning the basics, driving with his dad in fields and private yards for three years already.

However he thinks the new rules will not suit young people who live in rural areas, who don't have access to public transport and rely heavily on lifts.

"There's hardly any transport links out here so you sort of have to rely on people giving me lifts," he said.

"We're about five miles out from the nearest transport hub and it's just hard to organise lifts even to get to work or college."

Tommy has his own car ready to go and considers himself a confident driver who would pass his test first time, but said the time he has to wait to drive it has now been "extended".

"It is a bit gutting, because I was so excited until they announced the new rules coming in, it's hard to believe how big of a change it is going to be," he added.

While he recognises that something needs to be done to address the number of deaths on the roads there is a level of frustration for Adam, who is also from Omagh, about the minimum six-month delay to him getting behind the wheel.

"I'm really eager to get out on the road, especially since I've been hassling my parents. I go to the gym quite frequently, maybe four days a week, and it's straight after tech.

"If I can get up off my own two feet, get into my own car, and go to my gym by myself, it's nobody's problem but mine.

"All I used to talk about in high school was 'oh, what car are you getting', 'where are we going on a road trip', and now there's just more complications, it's just bummed everybody out," he added.

Moss is already learning to drive, so the new rules will not affect him, but he thinks it is a positive move because "you'll get a lot more confidence and a lot more experiences in different kinds of situations which will be really useful".

"Starting to drive by yourself can be a scary thing", so "if it's to help with safety I think its worth it," he added.

He recognises that some people are annoyed about the new rules, particularly the six-month wait, but thinks "in the long run, does it really matter if you get your test six months later? It's not that big of a deal".

The Police Service of Northern Ireland's (PSNI's) road safety lead Ch Supt Sam Donaldson said that in Northern Ireland "more people per head of population are involved in collisions, basic collisions, serious injury collisions, and sadly, fatal collisions, than any other part of the UK".

He has "no doubt" that it will save lives.

"Sadly the reality is that young and inexperienced drivers are disproportionately involved in more collisions.

"Some are minor, some are serious, and some sadly are result in fatalities as well."

Veronica Weir, who has 26 years' experience as a driving instructor thinks the law change is "terrific" and that young drivers can be irresponsible.

"It's been a long time coming, about 15 years in the pipeline.

"Kids today just think it's a video game, and if they crash, there's no consequences, there's no ripple effect, they'll just brush themselves off and drive off again," she said.

She said that dangerous driving can affect "their family, their insurance and other parts of the community".

The first new practical tests will take place on 1 April 2027.

For the minister behind the Department for Infrastructure reforms, Sinn Féin's Liz Kimmins, graduated driver licensing is about reducing the risks faced by those getting behind the wheel for the first time.

"I think what we've wanted to do here is shift that emphasis from just simply passing your driving test to actually becoming a confident and competent driver," she said.

articles.title: The AI telling farmers when to harvest
articles.summary: Will farmers want AI tools to help judge when to pick fruit, or is their own intuition enough?
articles.body:
When the first day of the apple harvest rolled around in Washington State last year, the fruit was ripe and the pickers were ready – but the weather had other ideas.

"It was like 38C… it's not safe for people to work in that heat," recalls Joel Carter at Okanagan Specialty Fruits. "We had to stop at 10 o'clock in the morning."

He says that artificial intelligence (AI) models that forecast ideal harvest dates, taking into account the weather, would be useful. "You need to know more than just when your fruit is going to be ripe. How long do you have to pick it?" he says. "That's where these models are really helpful."

Carter's company has more than 1,250 acres of apple orchards in Washington, and the fruit is grown for sliced apple portions – often sold to hotels and schools, for example. The firm is investing in technology with the hope of maximising productivity. Even the apples are genetically engineered so that they don't brown easily once cut.

But planning a harvest is tricky. New tools that count and analyse fruit on the tree or vine, and predict when crops will ripen, are emerging. It matters because prices for fruit, especially high-value berries such as strawberries or blueberries can fluctuate wildly. Getting the harvest date wrong means you book seasonal workers when you don't actually need them, and risk missing out on the biggest profits.

Okanagan Specialty Fruits is already experimenting with cameras from a Canadian firm called Vivid Machines. The cameras are mounted atop tractors and they scoop up imagery of the apple trees as the tractor trundles by. AI identifies buds, flowers or fruit in that footage.

"Right now, Vivid is telling us crop estimates and harvest dates," says Carter. He notes that the system is good at picking out very tiny flower buds, which are hard to see at a glance with the naked eye.

But the accuracy of forecasts is noticeably dependent on the quality of historical information fed in to the system, adds Carter. "This isn't something where an AI can scrape the internet and figure out what's the average [yield] for Granny Smith," he explains. "It's going to be bespoke to your farm."

Apples are at least somewhat forgiving – the harvest window for those Granny Smiths is three weeks long, says Carter. For other fruit, such as berries, you might only have a few days.

"If a strawberry crop is on, you have to harvest it – otherwise your entire crop gets diseased very, very quickly," says Raymond Martin, co-founder and chief operating officer of FruitCast, a UK company that offers harvest forecasts to fruit growers here.

His firm offers growers crop predictions for strawberries and also raspberries, blackberries, blueberries and tomatoes. "We're moving on to grapes next year," adds Martin.

Don't experienced farmers know when their fruit will be ripe, I ask? Martin says they generally do – but not necessarily across their entire farm, which might be many acres in size, or have both outdoor and indoor growing areas. "We do exactly what the farmers could do but we just do it on a scale that they can't."

The system analyses footage of ripening fruit that can be captured by drones, someone walking up and down a field with a smartphone, or a camera mounted on a farm vehicle.

This year has been challenging, notes Martin, with hot weather and severe drought hitting much of the UK . This has stressed many fruit plants, putting them into thermal dormancy and slowing down fruit production.

The FruitCast model accounts for weather and irrigation conditions in its forecasts. The company says, "our forecasts land within 10% of actual picked volume one week out (90% accurate) and within 17% three weeks out (83% accurate). We guarantee less than 20% error…"

Angus Soft Fruits is one company that has worked with FruitCast. AI tech for forecasting fruit ripeness is not yet "a finished solution" says operations director Neill Finlayson: "This journey is still ongoing and, whilst significant progress has been made, the industry remains some way from achieving a fully integrated forecasting ecosystem."

Driscoll's, a California headquartered fruit seller with a big operation in the UK, also confirmed to BBC News that some of its independent fruit growers in the UK have used FruitCast's technology.

Researchers are also exploring new ways of analysing fruit in intense detail. Many farmers already use handheld brix meters to gauge the sugar content of their crop. These devices work by measuring how much light has changed direction, or refracted, after passing through a liquid – indicating the volume of solids present.

Some such meters use infrared light, meaning there's no need to cut into the fruit to take measurements. But Yasaman Ghasempour at Princeton University says millimetre waves, high frequency radio waves, can penetrate deeper "They basically respond very well to humidity, water [and sugar]," she says.

She and her students have come up with a millimetre wave-based ripeness detector that could be used by farmers – or even customers searching for perfectly ripe fruit in shops. Her students tried it out at a local market in New Jersey. "[Staff] there got kind of scared that we were doing something shady," laughs Ghasempour.

Such fine-grained analysis of fruit, if currently unripe, could also help inform forecasts of when it will be ripe.

But while some growers, such as Carter, are interested in trying out new tech, many will wonder whether investing in it is really worthwhile. "Adoption is very complicated," says Jing Zhang at North Carolina State University. "The grower has to have confidence in the research and whether or not it works."

Zhang has been working on a system to automatically count the number of blueberries captured in smartphone images of blueberry bushes.

The simplest systems need not be expensive. Kevin Wang at the University of Florida has developed another crop-counting tool that can harvest imagery from $100 (£74) drones.

In the future, such information could feed in to ripeness predictions. However, he points out that some farmers might be uneasy about sharing commercially sensitive information about their growing strategies, such as fertiliser and irrigation plans, with third parties and AI models.

Ben Palone is senior director of automation and commercialisation at Western Growers, an association that represents farmers in the western US. He says harvest forecasts have some potential as "an optimisation tool".

But farmers will likely continue to rely on human intelligence. "Growers like to have people in the mix to make some of those very critical decisions – especially when it comes to harvests," he says.

articles.title: To Bengal plea on Congress pick, SC says will dismiss appeal
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Applying its recently framed policy of rejecting challenges to bails granted by high courts, Supreme Court on Wednesday told the West Bengal
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Applying its recently framed policy of rejecting challenges to bails granted by high courts, Supreme Court on Wednesday told the West Bengal govt that it would dismiss the state's appeal against grant of interim bail to Milan Pradhan, Congress candidate for the Nandigram assembly bypoll, who is an accused in a 2007 murder case.A CJI-led bench expressed difficulty to list the matter on Thursday and said, "Instead of Thursday, we will dismiss the appeal on Monday."By Monday, electioneering for the bypoll would be over and the state's appeal would be infructuous. Solicitor general Tushar Mehta, appearing for the state, requested a bench headed by CJI Surya Kant for a hearing on Thursday of the appeal challenging the grant of interim bail to Pradhan for canvassing for the election scheduled for Oct 6, campaigning for which will end on Oct 4.When the bench said since the HC had granted only interim bail, it would not entertain such an appeal, Mehta brought up Pradhan's history sheet -- accused in a murder case and featuring in six other FIRs on serious crimes -- to request a hearing on Thursday.The HC had, citing the relief the SC gave to AAP leader Arvind Kejriwal, granted bail to Pradhan on Tuesday and asked him to surrender before the additional chief judicial magistrate, Haldia, on Oct 21.Counting of votes in Nandigram, which was vacated by chief minister Suvendu Adhikari who also won from Bhabanipur, will happen on Oct 9.The state said in its appeal, "The HC granted interim bail to Pradhan, an accused charged with multiple counts of heinous offences including murder, arson, bomb blasts and rioting with deadly weapons, solely on the untenable pretext of permitting him to participate in an election."It added, "The HC completely disregarded settled principles governing the grant of bail, overlooked the respondent's continuous evasion of judicial process for nearly two decades, ignored his active subversion of the criminal justice system, and exposed prosecution witnesses to imminent danger."Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Nicolas Cage met Alice Kim while she was working as a waitress: How one chance encounter in a Los Angeles restaurant became a marriage
articles.summary: Before Nicolas Cage became a father of three, married five times, and found himself at the centre of some of Hollywood's most unconventional love stories,
articles.body: Before Nicolas Cage became a father of three, married five times, and found himself at the centre of some of Hollywood's most unconventional love stories, there was Alice Kim, who was a young waitress he met almost by chance at a Los Angeles restaurant in 2004.Picture it: 2004, Los Angeles. Cage, just off his third marriage, walked into the restaurant where Alice Kim was working. By any Hollywood standard, that’s barely a blip on the romance radar: a celebrity stopping for dinner. Yet the next few months would turn their shared moment into the kind of whirlwind even movies can’t quite capture.Per the Los Angeles Times, Cage was forty, a major star with a career full of unique roles and wild stories. Kim was about twenty at that first meeting: a sharp, seemingly regular young woman doing her job on the L.A. restaurant scene. Different backgrounds, different worlds. They hit it off in February, got engaged mere weeks later, and before summer showed up, they were married.How did Nicolas Cage meet Alice Kim?Cage’s version of their first encounter is about as quirky as he is. He told the Associated Press that it was a quick, awkward meeting at a nightclub (not just a restaurant, depending on who you ask). According to him, Kim vanished from the conversation after just five minutes. Cage, being Cage, wrote her a note, handed over his number, and waited to see what happened next.The real surprise wasn’t just the speed; it was how well the relationship stuck. According to the LA Times, the couple got engaged around April and married by July, holding a private ceremony at a ranch in Northern California. They kept the big day quiet: no media spectacle, just family and close friends.Their whirlwind engagement and weddingThere was also a practical reason for the quick wedding. Cage had to shoot ‘Lord of War’ in South Africa. Getting hitched meant Kim could travel with him for the production. That blend of necessity and romance probably helped them dodge some of the usual Hollywood drama, at least at first.There was chatter, of course. Cage was almost twice Kim’s age. But he brushed off questions about the difference, focusing instead on how marrying someone from another culture challenged and inspired him. He even joked (only half-joking) in a 2013 interview with The Guardian that marrying Kim was his way of “marrying outside the zip code.”From a whirlwind to building a familyThe whirlwind gave way to a new chapter in October 2005 when their son, Kal-El, was born. Yes, the name was Cage’s playful nod to Superman, whose Kryptonian name is Kal-El. It was his second child (he already had Weston with ex Christina Fulton), but his first with Kim. Parenthood changed him, as Cage has said that no movie role ever kept him away from his kids for more than a handful of days.What happened to Nicolas Cage and Alice Kim's marriage?His marriage with Kim turned out to be Cage’s longest, lasting over a decade together, which, to be honest, is basically a Hollywood eternity. And, of course, their time wasn’t drama-free. In 2011, police arrested Cage in New Orleans after an argument with Kim turned heated. He was accused of grabbing her arm during an argument on a French Quarter sidewalk, thrown in jail for the night, and released soon after. No charges stuck, and they carried on for years after.By 2016, though, things had changed. Cage’s rep confirmed their separation that June, ending eleven years of marriage. The split, surprisingly, didn’t turn ugly. Cage later called it a “shocker,” like something he didn’t see coming, but said he held no grudge.Looking back, Cage’s romance with Kim stands out. Five marriages, lots of wild tales, but with Kim, he found a partnership that lasted the longest. Kim and Cage stayed friends, mostly for their son’s sake, and when he married his fifth wife, Riko Shibata, in 2021, Kim and Kal-El celebrated with them. That evolved equation says a lot in a town where divorces can get messier than movie sets.
